name: Mass Timber
summary: Buildings of engineered wood. Cross-laminated and glued timber panels and beams make floors, walls and frames, and tall buildings of 6 to 25 storeys with warm interiors and a low carbon footprint.

philosophy.core_thesis: A building can be made of engineered timber panels and beams, and so store carbon, build fast off site and show the warm grain of its own structure.
design_principles: Use cross-laminated timber panels of 0.1 to 0.3m for floors and walls, and glulam beams and columns on a grid of 6 to 9m.
Show the timber: leave the soffit, the beam and the column visible, with fire-char allowances of 40 to 60mm.
Prefabricate in the factory, and lift the panels to the site in a plan with a tolerance of 2 to 5mm.
Keep the grid regular and repeating, because the panel and the truck size set the module.
Protect the timber from water: use a deep eave, a rainscreen and a ventilated cavity of 20 to 40mm.
Combine with a concrete core or hybrid floor for stiffness and fire when the building passes 8 storeys.
anti_patterns: Timber hidden behind plasterboard on every surface
A grid so irregular that each panel is unique
Open timber end grain exposed to the rain
Fake wood-pattern cladding on a steel frame
Long untreated timber spans without fire design
Dark opaque finishes that hide the grain

massing.form: A regular rectangular block of 6 to 25 storeys, with stacked floors and a timber grid on the facade.
massing.proportion: A bay of 6 to 9m by 6 to 9m; storey height of 3.0 to 3.6m; a plan of 15 to 25m deep.
massing.roof: A flat roof with a timber panel deck and a deep overhang, or a green roof.
massing.relation_to_ground: A concrete or masonry base keeps the timber 0.3 to 0.5m above the ground and out of the splash zone.

structure.system: Cross-laminated timber floors and walls, glulam beams and columns, often with a concrete core.
structure.span_and_module: A grid of 6 to 9m; slab span of 5 to 8m; CLT thickness of 0.1 to 0.3m; glulam sections 0.2 by 0.4m.
structure.expression: The glulam column, the beam and the panel edge are the structure and the interior, and they are left visible.

materials.finish: Natural and warm: sealed or oiled timber with visible grain, and char or clear sealer outside.

facade.composition: A regular timber frame facade: storey bands, vertical timber mullions and panel joints show the grid.
facade.openings: Large framed windows in panel bays; the window-to-wall ratio is 35 to 60%.

light_and_space.daylight: Daylight reaches 6 to 9m into the plan, and the timber soffit warms the light.
light_and_space.spatial_sequence: An open plan on a 6 to 9m grid, with a lobby, a stair and the open floor plates stacked in a regular order.
light_and_space.interior_character: A ceiling of 2.8 to 3.4m with visible glulam beams, panel soffits and a warm smell and tone.

ornament.attitude: There is no applied ornament: the grain, the panel joint and the connector are the detail.

rules.rule: Repeat the structural bay along the facade.
Hold the bay near a square, set by the panel and the truck.
Stack the services in one concrete core, away from the open floor.
Hold one structural timber on the whole facade.
Layer the rainscreen, the vent cavity, the panel and the fire char.
Keep the storey at a human height of 3.0 to 3.6m.

emotion.target_response: Warmth and care: the viewer feels a calm, natural, human-scale building that is also modern.

avoid_when: The brief asks for a wide open span of more than 20m or a deep wet basement.
The brief asks for a thin glass curtain wall.

modifiers.how: Lower the block to 2 or 3 storeys, add a pitched roof and a white plaster plinth, and warm the plan.
Let a script shape the panel edges into curves, with a free timber lattice.

sources.title: Andrew Waugh, Anthony Thistleton and Michael Green, Tall Timber Buildings (Routledge, 2022)
